name: Adam Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m from the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. This is confidential. What is your normal day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m 43, newly in charge of four people who handle product returns for a large furniture maker. I check damage photos, approve or reject claims and call the warehouse when a customer says a table never arrived. I use AI every day to sort photos and draft replies, but I still send the awkward cases to our best clerk. I like giving a customer a straight answer; I’m less good at forecasting the queue, and the team feels it when I get that wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What brought you into management, and what is home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I have a bachelor’s degree and worked on the returns desk for years before they gave me this junior manager post. My wife, Ruth, works mornings at a bakery; our children are seven and fourteen, and the mortgage and school costs leave us about two weeks of expenses saved. My pay is low for management, and there are few offices like this nearby. My father runs a small vehicle garage, but I wouldn’t count on him paying a manager’s wage; I’d rather learn a trade and earn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the team to use a photo sorter if it catches damage, but to keep talking to the customer when a delivery is disputed. I’d rather own a mistaken refund than hide behind a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep earning, which matters more to us than whether the software impresses anyone. Ruth’s bakery hours can drop and our savings barely cover a fortnight, so the mortgage still sits in my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I’d keep the morning returns board and test my photo sorter against the clerk’s decisions before sending replies. In the first year Ruth and I would skip one paid weekend outing each month and put the 45 aside for the next school bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about the family budget, not about AI in this picture. A quiet season at the bakery would still be rough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which school bill is coming next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our older child needs a new uniform coat. I can cover it if we stop spending the 45 before the invoice lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who makes the final call on a disputed delivery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do, after the warehouse and the clerk have checked the record. The customer should get a person’s name on the decision.

A **photo sorter** should be checked against the clerk’s decisions.
think: My **manager pay** continues in a plateau.
Ruth’s changing **bakery hours** keep the mortgage tight.
A **school coat** is large against a two-week reserve.
do: Keep the **morning board** and compare photo sorting with clerk decisions.
Skip one **paid outing** monthly and reserve 45 for school costs.
feel: I feel **anxious** about our small reserve.

fieldNote: He uses **AI daily** but checks it with a more experienced clerk.

His plan diverts **45 monthly** from outings to a uniform bill.

steps.text: Keep the morning returns board and check AI photo sorting against clerk decisions
Skip one paid weekend outing monthly to free 45 for school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the company will use AI for refund decisions, so staff must see the wrong calls before the team shrinks. I’d ask for a clear place to challenge a refused return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The sorting and replies are most of my day, and I’m the least experienced manager here. They could join our desk to another team and keep its manager, even if I run a good trial.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d compare AI decisions with one hundred closed return cases, including missing-delivery claims. In the first year I’d finish the company’s paid course on appeals, train myself on its audit screen and ask my director for a posted role handling contested refunds if the desk is merged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, maybe close to alarmed, because the mortgage needs this wage. I’d rather bring the errors to my director than wait to be called into an office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Ruth about the possible merger now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, after dinner when the children are doing homework. She would want to know what pay is at risk before we agree to any holiday plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the appeals role pays less?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for the written salary and compare it with the mortgage and Ruth’s usual hours. A job title does not make a short paycheck longer.

AI will handle **routine refund decisions** in our office.
think: My **new manager post** could go in a merger.
A strong trial may still leave the company choosing **another manager**.
do: Test **one hundred old claims** against AI decisions now.
Complete a **paid appeals course** and seek a posted appeals role at a viable wage.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing mortgage-covering pay.
S1.quote: A job title does not make a short paycheck longer.
fieldNote: His **junior standing** exposes him in a merged team.
He tests AI on **missing deliveries**, not just clear damage photos.
His next role requires **posted work** and written pay covering bills.

steps.text: Compare AI decisions against one hundred closed return and missing-delivery cases

Apply for a posted contested-refunds role only if written pay covers household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say workers need dates and written severance terms before the returns desk is handed to a system. I’d tell customers who will answer a disputed refund when the office is smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 would do the checking and customer replies that make up my job, likely better than I can. Physical repair work at my father’s garage might last until robots arrive around 2031, but two weeks of savings will not pay the mortgage while I learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tonight Ruth and I would cancel the planned trip and list mortgage, food and school costs. Before 2028 I’d ask my father whether his garage has a paid apprentice vacancy and enroll in a vehicle service course only if the company or garage covers the fee and paid time; in the first year after AGI arrives, I’d take garage work only with a written wage that covers our mortgage share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m alarmed. I can learn new tools, but I cannot rebuild my wage in two years just by being willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your father help if the garage cannot pay that wage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He could probably watch the children one afternoon, but I would ask first and not make it his regular duty. I would keep looking for paid work rather than put my father’s garage into debt for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Ruth say about the trip?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ruth would agree if we knew where the saved trip money was going. We would tell the children that a mortgage payment comes before a holiday ticket.

say: I’d ask for **written dates and terms** before a desk closure.
Customers need a **named appeal contact** after automation.
think: A garage bridge before **2031 robots** still needs a real wage.
do: Cancel the **family trip** after reviewing bills with Ruth.
Ask about a **paid garage vacancy** and take funded training only if time is paid.
feel: I feel **alarmed** by the two-year wage risk.
S2.quote: I would keep looking for paid work rather than put my father’s garage into debt for me.
fieldNote: His father’s garage is a **possible paid route**, not guaranteed employment.
The **2028 thinking change** precedes 2031 hands-on robots.
He requires **funded fees and time** plus a mortgage-covering written wage.

Take garage work after 2028 only with written pay covering his mortgage share

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough to publish real retraining offers and let people finish an apprenticeship before the desk changes. I’d still want customers to know where a refused return goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn vehicle servicing while I keep my salary, if a garage offers a proper place. Robots come to hands-on work around 2034, so I would treat the trade as a few years of earning, not a promise forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I’d enroll in a paid evening vehicle-service program if Ruth can handle school pickup and the fee is covered. I’d work one paid Saturday a month at my father’s garage if he has work for me, then apply for a posted service technician opening before 2031 only if the wage covers the mortgage; in the first year after AGI, I’d remain only while paid hands-on repair work exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but five years gives me time to find out whether I’m any good with engines. I would not resign from management until a real offer is in my hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your father has no Saturday work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I’d practise in the program and ask other garages about a paid placement. Family is a place to ask, not a blank wage cheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if Ruth cannot do pickup?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d move the course to another term rather than leave our youngest waiting at school. She has her own bakery shift to protect.

Customers need a **return appeal route** during the transition.
Five years gives people time to **finish apprenticeships**.
think: A vehicle trade could provide **some earnings** before 2034 robots.
I need a **proper placement** and an offer before leaving management.

Work **paid Saturdays** if the garage has work and seek a mortgage-covering opening.

fieldNote: He treats family help as **conditional**, never free labor.

steps.text: Enroll in paid vehicle-service training only if Ruth covers school pickup and fees are funded

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a decade lets employers offer apprenticeships and customers a real appeals route without rushing. I’d ask for clear dates rather than a speech about opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 53 in 2036 and might have a stronger trade and more savings by then. I’m still aware that robots arrive around 2039 and can do hands-on work too, so the garage is not a permanent refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting January 2027 Ruth and I would transfer 60 monthly to savings only when her bakery hours reach their usual level. I’d take a funded service course within two years, work paid Saturdays if my father has jobs, and apply for a written garage offer before 2036 only if its pay meets our mortgage; in the first year after AGI, I’d stay only while the work remains paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the deadline, but ten years gives us time to build a cushion before I change trades. I would still count the pay, not just the years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take over your father’s garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if he wanted to sell and the accounts showed it could pay us without borrowing against our house. I am not putting the mortgage behind a family handshake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell them I may work some Saturdays to save money for the house. I would not make them responsible for whether the garage succeeds.

Customers need a **real appeal route** during the change.
I’d ask for **clear dates** instead of vague promises.
think: I could build **savings and trade skill** by age 53.
The **2039 robots** mean repair work is not forever.
do: Save **60 monthly** only when Ruth’s bakery hours hold.
Seek a **mortgage-covering garage offer**; consider ownership only if Dad sells and accounts support wages without home borrowing.

feel: I feel **uneasy** but have time to build a cushion.
S4.quote: I am not putting the mortgage behind a family handshake.
fieldNote: The savings transfer depends on **Ruth’s usual bakery hours**.
The garage path needs **funded training** and written adequate pay.
Any **takeover** needs his father’s consent and accounts supporting wages without home borrowing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the mortgage cannot wait for me to finish an apprenticeship. A real paid place, a written wage and enough notice to arrange Ruth’s shifts would help. I would ask my father for a chance, but I would not ask him to carry our household.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn’t ask who signs the refusal when the returns desk is gone. A refused refund still reaches somebody’s kitchen table as a bill.

headlineQuote: A refused refund still reaches somebody’s kitchen table as a bill.
portrait: **Adam**, 43, is a junior returns manager with a bachelor’s degree and daily AI use.
His low pay and **two-week reserve** strain a mortgage and two children.
He favors **earned apprenticeships** and checks whether family work can really pay.
He tests **garage training** while protecting Ruth’s shifts and the mortgage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his returns job before a paid trade place is ready.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship**, written wage and enough notice to arrange Ruth’s shifts would help.
